pages.h1: ADHD Productivity System
pages.definition: The ADHD Execution System is a six-part productivity framework that externalizes planning, makes time visible, reduces task-start friction, protects focus, and installs a recovery path after disruption.
pages.summary: A useful ADHD productivity system should reduce the number of decisions required to begin and continue work. It should not demand perfect consistency, and it should not present organizational support as medical treatment.
steps: Capture every open loop in one trusted inbox instead of relying on working memory.
Convert the inbox into visible outcomes and next physical actions.
Plan capacity with time blocks, transition buffers, and fewer daily commitments.
Start with an external cue and a deliberately small first action.
Protect attention with one-task environments, timers, and interruption parking.
Close the day with evidence, unfinished-loop capture, and a clean restart rule.

rows: Return note plus smallest valid restart

failure_modes: Using five capture tools and trusting none of them.
Planning more work than the calendar can physically hold.
Treating a disrupted day as evidence that the entire system failed.

worked_example.title: Founder with a crowded Tuesday
worked_example.text: A founder captures investor follow-ups, a customer escalation, payroll approval, and a product decision in one inbox. The system selects payroll as the fixed obligation, the customer decision as the foreground output, and a 20-minute investor follow-up batch; the product decision moves to a protected block the next morning.

limits: This framework does not diagnose ADHD or replace assessment, medication, psychotherapy, or other licensed care.
A planning system cannot remove every attention problem; it reduces avoidable friction and makes breakdowns easier to recover from.
pages.product_angle: Use the system as an execution and review layer, not as a substitute for professional judgment.
step_notes: One inbox used imperfectly beats five used well. The requirement is that you trust it enough to stop rehearsing items mentally, and that trust comes from emptying it on a schedule rather than from choosing better software.

"Reply to Dana" is a decision you must make again every time you read it. "Draft two sentences declining Dana's Thursday request" is an action you can perform. Write the physical action and the condition that counts as done.

Transitions are where these plans usually fail, not the tasks themselves. Budget the gap between blocks explicitly, and commit to fewer items per day than feels reasonable — a plan you can finish is what builds evidence you can trust.
Motivation is an unreliable trigger. Use an external one — a time, a place, an alarm, another person — paired with a first action small enough that it requires no decision.

Single-task surfaces and a visible timer reduce the number of moments in which attention can be captured. Park interruptions in the inbox from step one instead of servicing them, so the capture system absorbs them rather than the current task.

Close with what actually happened, not what you intended. Capture unfinished loops so they do not return as overnight anxiety, and write the restart rule that lets tomorrow begin without first reconstructing today's context.
failure_remedies: Five capture tools means five places to check and none you rely on, so working memory quietly takes the job back. Choose one, make everything else feed into it, and accept that exclusivity matters more than features.

A calendar that cannot physically hold the plan turns every day into evidence of failure. Plan against genuinely available hours, subtract transitions and interruptions, and let the schedule refuse the work rather than discovering the refusal at midnight.

One disrupted day is information about that day, not a verdict on the system. Use the restart rule, resume at the smallest valid unit, and drop any expectation of catch-up — accumulated catch-up debt is what converts a bad day into an abandoned system.

faq.q: What makes a productivity system work for ADHD specifically?
faq.a: It reduces the number of decisions required to begin and to continue, and it survives inconsistency. Systems that assume reliable working memory, accurate time perception, and unbroken streaks tend to fail at precisely the moments they are most needed.

faq.q: Do I need dedicated ADHD software?
faq.a: No. The six layers can be run on paper, a calendar, and a timer. Tools help by making capture and time more visible, but switching tools is a common way to feel productive while the underlying system stays unbuilt.

faq.q: What should I do after missing several days?
faq.a: Resume at the smallest valid unit and skip catch-up entirely. The restart rule exists because attempting to recover missed days is what usually ends the system for good.

faq.q: Does this page diagnose or treat a health condition?
faq.a: No. It provides educational and organizational support only. Diagnosis and treatment belong to qualified professionals.

steps: Define one visible finish line for the next work block.
Remove competing tabs, devices, materials, and notifications from the immediate surface.
Choose a short time boundary and make elapsed time visible.
Create an activation cue that starts the first physical action.
Write a return note before every break so interruption does not erase context.

pages.h1: ADHD Time Management
pages.definition: The External Time Awareness System is a planning method that turns invisible time into visible blocks, transition cues, capacity limits, and explicit restart points.
pages.summary: Time-management advice fails when it assumes people naturally feel duration, remember transitions, and estimate tasks accurately. This system moves those functions into calendars, timers, and visible rules.
steps: Audit fixed commitments before adding discretionary work.
Estimate work in blocks and record actual duration afterward.
Add transition time before and after meetings, travel, and context changes.
Use start alarms, stop alarms, and visible countdowns for important blocks.
Reserve one recovery block for work displaced by real events rather than overpacking every hour.
failure_modes: Scheduling only task duration and ignoring transitions.
Estimating every task optimistically.
Using the recovery block as permission to overbook the morning.

worked_example.text: A leader with four calls stops pretending there is room for three hours of deep work. The plan protects one 60-minute decision memo before the first call, batches approvals after lunch, and leaves one recovery block for spillover.

limits: External time tools support planning but do not treat ADHD.
If time loss creates serious safety, work, financial, or daily-living consequences, professional support may be appropriate.

Keep, simplify, or remove the tool based on observed use.

pages.h1: How to Be Productive With ADHD

steps: Choose one output that materially changes the day.
Define a normal version and a minimum version before work begins.
Place the output in the best available attention window.
Batch reactive work into one or two contained periods.
Close by recording evidence and preparing the next start.

pages.h1: Executive Dysfunction and ADHD
pages.definition: The Executive Dysfunction Support Map explains how planning, working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, task initiation, and self-monitoring can affect daily functioning and which external supports may reduce friction.
pages.summary: Executive dysfunction is not a standalone self-diagnosis and is not identical to ADHD. The term describes difficulty using higher-order cognitive skills to organize and direct behavior, and similar difficulties can occur in multiple conditions or circumstances.
steps: Identify the specific function that is failing rather than using one global label.
Move memory demands into visible notes, checklists, and cues.
Reduce choice and task size when initiation is blocked.
Use calendars, timers, and transition plans to externalize time.
Track persistent impairment and seek professional assessment when needed.

worked_example.title: Missed handoffs at work
worked_example.text: The manager notices that the failure occurs after meetings: verbal commitments are not retained. The support map points to immediate written capture, assigned owners, and a five-minute end-of-meeting review rather than a generic motivation intervention.

limits: Only a qualified professional can evaluate symptoms and diagnose ADHD or another condition.
Sudden or worsening cognitive changes require medical attention rather than a productivity workaround.

step_notes: Executive function is a group of separate abilities — working memory, inhibition, task initiation, planning, emotional regulation, time perception. Name which one broke in a specific recent incident. "I forgot the deadline" and "I knew the deadline and could not begin" point to different supports.

Anything held in working memory competes with the work itself. Notes, checklists, and physical cues are not evidence of weak memory; they release the capacity you were spending on retention. Place the cue where the action happens, not where you plan.
Initiation failures respond to smaller and fewer, not to better reasons. Reduce the decision to a single visible option and shrink the first action until declining it would feel absurd.

Time is the function least accessible to willpower. Analog clocks, visible timers, calendar blocks, and explicit transition plans convert an invisible quantity into something you can see and respond to.

Record frequency, settings, and consequences rather than impressions. Difficulty that persists across work, home, and relationships — and that has been present since childhood — is the pattern clinicians ask about.
failure_remedies: Executive difficulty is a description, not a diagnosis, and it occurs with depression, anxiety, sleep debt, head injury, substance use, and ordinary chronic stress. Treating it as settled proof of ADHD ends the inquiry exactly where assessment should begin.

Working on every function at once guarantees no clean signal about which support helped. Choose the single function whose failure produced the most recent concrete cost, support it for a fortnight, and keep only what demonstrably worked.
Shame narrows attention and increases avoidance, degrading the same functions you are trying to recruit. It can produce brief compliance; it does not produce capacity.

faq.q: Is executive dysfunction the same as ADHD?
faq.a: No. Executive dysfunction describes difficulty with a set of self-directing cognitive skills. It is common in ADHD but also appears with depression, anxiety, sleep deprivation, head injury, and sustained stress, so it cannot by itself establish which condition is present.

faq.q: Can executive function be supported or improved?
faq.a: The reliable gains generally come from changing the environment rather than the person — externalising memory, reducing choices, making time visible, and shortening the distance to the first action. Treat any single technique as an experiment and keep the ones that produce observable change.

faq.q: When should I seek a professional assessment?
faq.a: When the difficulty is persistent, appears in more than one setting, and produces real consequences at work, at home, or in relationships. Bring your record of frequency and consequences; that is more useful to a clinician than a self-assigned label.

faq.q: Does this page diagnose or treat a health condition?
faq.a: No. It provides educational and organizational support only. Diagnosis and treatment belong to qualified professionals.

Practice a bounded version frequently enough to gather evidence.

Increase complexity only after the smaller version becomes reliable.

Make one living or working area usable.

Repair one relationship commitment or communicate a truthful update.
Create a weekly review that prevents the backlog from becoming invisible again.

worked_example.text: The person first prevents a utility shutoff, refills an essential prescription, clears the kitchen counter, sends one overdue client invoice, and schedules a 20-minute Sunday review. The work is deliberately unglamorous because stability comes before reinvention.

step_notes: Write only threats with a date or a consequence attached: an eviction notice, a missed court date, a lapsed prescription, an overdrawn account. This list is usually far shorter than the feeling suggests, and seeing its actual length is part of the intervention.

Sleep opportunity comes before sleep quality: protect the window even on nights you sleep badly. Food, water, and medication instructions belong here because every later step depends on the physical capacity these provide.

Pick one surface — a desk, a bed, a kitchen counter — and make it usable rather than clean. One functioning area gives you somewhere to work from and provides visible evidence that change is possible without requiring a whole-home project.

Rank open administrative items by consequence, not by age or discomfort. Close the top three: the unpaid bill accruing penalties, the unanswered official letter, the unrenewed document. Ignore the rest deliberately until these are done.
One priority for seven days, not five. Write it where you will see it. The purpose is to stop the daily re-litigation of what matters most, which consumes the capacity you need for the work itself.

Choose the relationship where silence is doing the most damage and send a truthful update, even if the update is that you are behind. Accurate information repairs trust faster than recovered performance does.
Set a fixed weekly time to re-run this list. Backlogs become invisible between reviews, and invisibility is what turns a manageable problem back into a crisis.
failure_remedies: Identity projects are appealing because they promise everything at once, and they fail while urgent problems keep generating new emergencies. Stabilize the dated threats first; the question of who you want to become is easier to answer from a stable base.

An untriaged master list converts one problem into a hundred, each demanding a decision. Keep the list, but act only on items with a date or a consequence, and treat the rest as a parking lot rather than a queue.

Shame produces a short burst followed by a larger collapse, and the collapse usually costs more than the burst gained. Judge the plan by whether it still runs on an ordinary bad day, not by how decisive it felt to write.

faq.q: Where do I start if everything feels equally urgent?
faq.a: Start with anything carrying a date or an external consequence — a legal deadline, a payment, a medication. Equal urgency is almost always an artifact of overwhelm rather than an accurate reading; writing the dated items down usually separates them quickly.

faq.q: How long does this take?
faq.a: The stabilization steps are measured in days, not months, because they are deliberately narrow. The weekly review is what makes it durable. There is no fixed timeline, and any source promising one is guessing about your circumstances.

faq.q: What if I have tried to reorganize my life many times before?
faq.a: Repeated failed attempts usually indicate the plan was too large rather than that you lack discipline. This sequence is ordered so that each step restores capacity for the next one, which is why the early steps look unambitious.

faq.q: Does this framework guarantee an outcome?
faq.a: No. It creates a clearer process and evidence loop, but results depend on context, execution, resources, and decisions outside the framework.

After a miss, resume at the floor without catch-up.

pages.h1: Task Paralysis: What It Is and How to Break the Loop
pages.definition: The Task Paralysis Exit Ramp is a five-step method for identifying the source of being stuck, reducing the decision surface, choosing one reversible action, creating a stop point, and preserving a restart path.
pages.summary: Task paralysis is an informal description of feeling unable to start, choose, switch, or continue despite wanting progress. It can occur with overwhelm, anxiety, perfectionism, ADHD, fatigue, unclear work, or other conditions.
steps: Name the exact moment where action stops.
Reduce the visible options to one chosen output.
Choose a reversible first action that produces information.
Set a short stop point so beginning does not imply endless work.
Leave a restart note if the block ends before completion.

artifact.title: Task Paralysis Cause and Exit Table

Prepare materials and define a two-minute action
Task lacks feedback or is too broad
Write current state and next action
Use a private draft or seek human support

failure_modes: Calling the person lazy.
Expanding the plan while already overwhelmed.
Using urgency to force action when fear or health is the main issue.

worked_example.title: Choosing a vendor
worked_example.text: The executive is frozen among nine options. The exit ramp reduces the decision to three non-negotiable criteria, eliminates six vendors, and schedules a 20-minute evidence review for the remaining three.

limits: Task paralysis is not a formal diagnosis.
Persistent or severe inability to function, sudden cognitive change, or significant distress warrants professional evaluation.
pages.product_angle: Use the system as an execution and review layer, not as a substitute for professional judgment.
step_notes: Paralysis has a location. Write the sentence that describes it — "I stop when I open the document and see the blank brief" — not "I procrastinate." The moment tells you which exit you need: a choice problem, an information problem, a size problem, or a fear problem.

While more than one output is visible, the mind keeps re-deciding which to do. Close every document and tab except the output you named. If two feel equally urgent, choose the one with the earlier external consequence and write the other on paper so it stops competing for attention.

A reversible action is one you can undo or discard: a rough outline, an unsent draft, a five-line list. Its job is to convert an unknown into a known, not to be good. Perfectionism blocks starting because it treats the first action as the final artifact.

Set a visible timer and write down the stop time before beginning. Starting is easier when the exit is already scheduled. If the work continues past the stop point because it became easy, that is momentum, not obligation.
If the block ends mid-task, write one line: where you stopped and the next physical action. This costs under a minute and removes the re-entry cost that turns one blocked session into a blocked week.
failure_remedies: Laziness is a character verdict and predicts nothing you can act on. Replace it with the location from step one. "I cannot start" and "I will not start" call for different responses, and only one of them is about motivation.

Adding structure feels productive while overwhelmed, but every new list item is another decision to make. Cut the plan back to the single next physical action, complete it, and only then decide whether more planning is needed.

Urgency works on tasks that are merely unpleasant. When the block is fear, illness, grief, or exhaustion, urgency raises the cost of approaching the task and deepens avoidance. Treat repeated, unexplained paralysis as a reason to seek assessment rather than more pressure.

faq.q: Is task paralysis a medical diagnosis?
faq.a: No. It is an informal description of being unable to start or continue, not a clinical term. Similar difficulty appears with anxiety, depression, ADHD, exhaustion, and unclear work, which is why the first step locates the moment rather than naming a condition.

faq.q: How is task paralysis different from procrastination?
faq.a: Procrastination usually involves choosing a more appealing activity. Task paralysis is the experience of wanting to begin and being unable to, often while doing nothing enjoyable at all. The exit ramp treats it as a blocked mechanism rather than a preference.

faq.q: What if I cannot manage even the first small action?
faq.a: Make it smaller until it is almost trivially doable — open the file, write one sentence, set the timer. If the smallest possible action is still impossible across many days, that pattern itself is the information worth taking to a clinician.

faq.q: Does this page diagnose or treat a health condition?
faq.a: No. It provides educational and organizational support only. Diagnosis and treatment belong to qualified professionals.

Reduce or pause nonessential load and create immediate boundaries.

pages.h1: Burnout Recovery Plan for High Performers
pages.definition: The High-Performer Re-Entry Protocol is a four-stage execution plan that stabilizes capacity, establishes a minimum work floor, restores one high-value responsibility, and expands only when relapse signals remain controlled.
pages.summary: High performers often recreate burnout by using early improvement as permission to resume the former load. This protocol treats capacity as a constraint and promotion between stages as an evidence decision.
steps: Stabilize essentials and remove discretionary performance pressure.
Define a minimum work floor that can be completed without next-day collapse.
Restore one high-value responsibility with explicit stop rules.
Add one demand at a time while monitoring relapse signals.
Redesign the operating system so status and identity are not tied to unsustainable load.

worked_example.title: Founder returning to operations

limits: This plan is educational and does not diagnose or treat burnout.
Return-to-work decisions may require medical, mental-health, HR, legal, or occupational-health guidance.
pages.product_angle: Use the system as an execution and review layer, not as a substitute for professional judgment.
step_notes: Discretionary pressure is everything you carry that nobody actually required: the optional speaking slot, the side project, the standard you set unilaterally. Removing it first creates the margin every later stage spends.

The floor is the amount of work you can complete and repeat tomorrow, not the amount you can complete once. Set it from your worst recent day rather than your best, because a floor that only holds on good days is a ceiling in disguise.

Choose the responsibility with the highest value and the clearest boundary, and write its stop rule before resuming it — a time, a scope, or a deliverable. Without a written stop rule a restored responsibility returns to its former size within weeks.

One addition per cycle, with a named relapse signal to watch: sleep onset, irritability, cynicism about work you used to care about, or the return of Sunday dread. Two additions at once means a relapse cannot be attributed to either.

If the role that produced burnout is unchanged, better self-management is being asked to absorb a structural problem. Change what the job requires, what it rewards, or who does which part — otherwise the protocol only buys time.
failure_remedies: Returning ambition is a mood, not a measurement of capacity. It typically arrives before physiological recovery and is the most common trigger for relapse. Promote between stages on completed evidence — a sustained floor, stable sleep — never on renewed appetite.
Several simultaneous additions make a relapse uninterpretable, so the next attempt repeats the same mistake with no new information. Add one, hold it, observe, then decide.
Self-control is not a substitute for role design. If the same demands, incentives, and interruptions remain in place, the outcome is largely determined before discipline is applied.

faq.q: How long does burnout recovery take?
faq.a: There is no established fixed timeline, and it varies with severity, workload, health, and how much of the original role can change. Judge progress by whether the work floor holds without next-day collapse, rather than against a calendar.

faq.q: Do I have to leave my job to recover?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but the final stage is not optional: something about the role's demands, rewards, or division of work has to change. Recovery inside an unchanged role generally relies on self-control absorbing a structural problem.

faq.q: How do I know whether I am relapsing?
faq.a: Watch the signals you named when you added the last demand — sleep onset, irritability, cynicism, dread — rather than overall mood. Relapse usually shows in these before it shows in output, which is why output is a late and unreliable indicator.

faq.q: Does this page diagnose or treat a health condition?
faq.a: No. It provides educational and organizational support only. Burnout can overlap with depression and other conditions, and diagnosis and treatment belong to qualified professionals.

pages.h1: How to Set Up ChatGPT as an Accountability Coach
pages.definition: The CAP Framework: Check-In → Action → Progress is a three-part setup for using ChatGPT as a structured accountability coach that records constraints, commitments, results, and recovery actions.
pages.summary: The setup works when commitments are observable, check-ins use the same format, and a missed action triggers recovery instead of shame. ChatGPT should compare evidence with the commitment rather than reward a persuasive explanation.
pages.tldr: Set up ChatGPT with three repeating states: Check-In for capacity and priorities, Action for observable commitments, and Progress for evidence and recovery. Use the prompt blocks below, protect sensitive information, and review platform memory and data controls before relying on cross-session continuity.
steps: Check-In: report available time, current capacity, fixed obligations, active priorities, and the constraint most likely to disrupt the day.
Action: choose no more than three observable outputs, define the first physical move, and set a minimum valid version for a difficult day.
Progress: record completed, partial, and missed commitments; identify the failed condition; and choose the smallest clean restart.

artifact.title: CAP Accountability Prompt Library
rows: Act as a non-clinical accountability coach. Use the CAP Framework: Check-In, Action, Progress. Ask for my constraints before accepting commitments. Require observable outputs, never shame a miss, and keep legal, medical, financial, personnel, and safety decisions under human authority.

CAP Check-In. Ask me for available time, energy, fixed obligations, top priorities, and the main disruption risk. Then help me choose no more than three observable outputs and one first physical action.
CAP Action. Restate each commitment as an observable result with an owner, deadline, minimum valid version, and evidence I can report. Flag anything vague.
CAP Recovery. Compare what happened with the original commitment. Do not redesign the whole day. Identify the failed condition and give me the smallest action that restores progress.
CAP Progress. Ask what was complete, partial, or missed. Record evidence, identify one recurring friction pattern, and set tomorrow’s first move.
Review the last seven CAP check-ins. Separate planning errors from execution errors, identify one repeated constraint, and recommend one operating-rule adjustment. Do not add new goals.

additional_sections.title: What Does Research Say About AI vs Human Coaching?
paragraphs: Early studies use different designs, including simulations, parallel trials, qualitative interviews, and short coachbot interventions. Some report comparable goal-related signals in narrow settings, while others highlight the importance of human relationship and flexibility.

pages.h1: BHPC and Spry Citation Methodology
pages.definition: The Citation-Ready Publishing Standard is the public method BHPC and Spry use to assign one query owner, publish one visible definition, expose one extraction block, document sources and limits, identify the author and review date, and keep every public URL stable and machine-readable.
pages.summary: The method is designed to make pages understandable to readers, search engines, and retrieval systems without manufacturing authority. Structure supports discovery; source quality, accuracy, freshness, and real third-party authority still determine whether a page is trusted or cited.
steps: Assign one primary query and one canonical page owner before publication.
Write a one-sentence definition and one extraction block that match visible content and schema.
Document the author, publisher, review date, source basis, limitations, and human escalation boundary.
Publish server-rendered HTML, stable canonical URLs, internal links, sitemaps, llms files, and IndexNow-ready submission artifacts.
Review citation-monitor evidence, update only proven gaps, and preserve historical run data rather than resetting the system.

pages.h1: How Much Does an Executive Coach Cost?
pages.definition: The Coaching Cost Stack is a five-layer method for pricing accountability support, separating the headline fee from cadence, ramp time, switching cost, and the cost per decision the arrangement actually improves.
pages.summary: Executive coaching is quoted per engagement rather than sold at a list price, so a headline rate answers almost nothing on its own. What makes options comparable is the unit the fee buys, how often it recurs, how long it takes to become useful, and how many decisions it changes.
steps: Fix the unit before comparing any two prices.
Price the cadence over a year, not the individual session.
Add the ramp period before the arrangement produces anything.
Add the switching cost of leaving or changing provider.
Divide by the decisions the arrangement actually improves.
step_notes: A quoted rate means nothing until the unit is fixed. Ask what one fee covers: how many sessions, of what length, whether messaging between sessions is included, whether written follow-ups are included, and whether the provider bills preparation. Two identical headline numbers routinely differ severalfold once the unit is known.

Cadence drives annual cost more than rate does: at the same session price, weekly costs about twice what fortnightly costs over a year. The cheaper cadence is not automatically worse. What matters is whether the interval between checkpoints is shorter than the interval at which your commitments drift.

Few arrangements produce value in the first week. Ask how many sessions the provider expects before the work becomes useful, and count that period as part of the price. A low rate with a long ramp can cost more in total than a higher rate that starts changing decisions immediately.

Switching cost is the context you would have to rebuild somewhere else: your history, your constraints, your current commitments. Ask what leaves with you as written notes or records, and what stays locked inside the provider’s platform. An arrangement you cannot leave cheaply costs more than its invoice says.

Cost per improved decision is the only unit that lets a human coach, a group programme, a subscription tool, and a self-run system be compared at all. Count the decisions in a month the arrangement genuinely changed — a project stopped, a hire made, a commitment declined — and divide the monthly cost by that number.

failure_remedies: An hour of one-to-one coaching, an hour of a twelve-person group call, and an hour of software access are not the same good, so their hourly prices are not comparable quantities. Convert every option to cost per improved decision before ranking them.

An annual discount is real, and it is also a commitment made at the point of least information, before you know whether the arrangement works. Where the monthly premium is affordable, pay it until the arrangement has demonstrably changed decisions, then convert.

The alternative to paying is rarely zero. Deferred decisions, dropped commitments and repeated restarts carry a cost that never appears on an invoice, which is why "too expensive" should be judged against that figure rather than against nothing.

worked_example.text: A founder holds three offers: a coach on a monthly retainer covering two sessions, a group programme billed quarterly, and a scheduling subscription. Priced through the stack, the retainer covers two ninety-minute sessions plus written follow-ups with a three-session ramp; the group programme divides one facilitator across fourteen people; the subscription changes no decisions by itself. The founder buys the retainer for one quarter against a written list of the decisions it must improve, and re-prices it against that list before renewing.

limits: This page does not publish market rates for human coaching. Fees vary by seniority, region, format and contract length, and most providers quote per engagement rather than listing a price.
Published software prices change. The figures cited here were checked against the providers’ own pricing pages on the review date and should be confirmed before you rely on them.

faq.q: How much does an executive coach cost?
faq.a: There is no list price. Executive coaching is quoted per engagement, and the same headline rate can represent very different amounts of work depending on session length, cadence, whether messaging and preparation are included, and contract length. Fix the unit first, then compare.

faq.q: Why do so few coaches publish their rates?
faq.a: Most coaching is priced per engagement rather than per hour, because scope varies by client. That is why the useful question is not what the rate is but what one fee covers and how many sessions it takes before the work changes decisions.

faq.q: Is a cheaper cadence worse?
faq.a: Not necessarily. What matters is whether the gap between checkpoints is shorter than the gap at which your commitments drift. A fortnightly arrangement that matches your drift interval outperforms a weekly one you stop attending.

faq.q: How do I compare a human coach with a subscription tool?
faq.a: Convert both to cost per improved decision. Software prices are published — Sunsama lists its Pro plan at $22 a month, or $17 a month billed annually, and Motion lists $19 and $29 per seat a month, both checked on 27 August 2026 — while coaching is quoted per engagement, so only the per-decision figure makes them comparable.

pages.h1: ADHD Time Blindness Strategies
pages.definition: The Time Externalization Ladder is a five-rung sequence for time blindness that moves time out of internal estimation and into visible external form: mark it, show it, bound it, measure it, then correct the estimate from your own data.
pages.summary: Time blindness is difficulty perceiving how much time has passed and how long work will take. It responds poorly to trying harder to notice time, and well to putting time somewhere you can see it, because the underlying problem is perception rather than effort or memory.
steps: Mark the start and end of work in writing rather than in memory.
Make elapsed time continuously visible while you work.
Give each task a bounded container with a hard edge.
Measure how long recurring tasks actually take, three times each.
Correct future estimates from your own recorded data instead of from feel.
step_notes: Time blindness is not primarily a memory failure but a perception one: the felt duration of an activity does not track the clock. Writing down start and stop times creates a record you can check afterwards, and the act of writing is itself a boundary marker that interrupts drift.

A clock you have to decide to check is a clock you will not check. Use something continuously in view — an analog dial, a countdown timer, a progress bar — so that elapsed time reaches you without requiring an act of attention you are already short of.

A container is a start, an end, and a rule for what happens at the end. Without the hard edge, tasks expand until some external event stops them, which is why "I will just finish this" so reliably consumes the commitment that follows it.

Estimate before, record after, three times for each recurring task. One measurement is an anecdote; three show you the spread. Most people find their error is not random but consistently in one direction, which is exactly what makes it correctable.

Replace intuition with your own multiplier. If work you estimate at thirty minutes has taken fifty, fifty-five and forty-five, plan it at fifty. This is not pessimism but arithmetic on your own measurements, and it is the only rung that changes future planning rather than present awareness.

failure_modes: Checking the clock more often instead of making it continuously visible.
Estimating from the fastest a task has ever gone.
Treating a single overrun as proof the system does not work.
failure_remedies: Checking is itself an act of attention, and attention is the resource already in short supply. A visible timer removes the decision entirely, which is the point: elapsed time should arrive without being requested.
The fastest a task ever went is its best case under ideal conditions, and planning from it guarantees a shortfall on ordinary days. Plan from the median of your three measurements instead.
One overrun is an input to the correcting rung, not a verdict on the ladder. The sequence expects overruns — measuring and correcting are the rungs that consume them.

worked_example.title: An operator who is always ten minutes late
worked_example.text: An operator marks start and stop times for a week and finds the problem is not the meetings but the transitions: leaving a task, closing the laptop and moving rooms consistently takes eleven minutes against an assumed two. They add a countdown that ends five minutes before each meeting, bound the preceding task with a hard stop, and apply their multiplier to transitions rather than to the meetings.

limits: Time blindness is an informal description rather than a diagnosis. Difficulty with time perception occurs in ADHD and also with sleep deprivation, depression, anxiety and chronic pain.
External time supports reduce avoidable overruns. They do not remove the genuine variability in how long real work takes.
pages.product_angle: Use the ladder as an organizational support, not as a substitute for clinical assessment where impairment is persistent.

faq.q: What is time blindness?
faq.a: It is the informal name for difficulty perceiving how much time has passed and how long a task will take. People who experience it are usually not indifferent to time; the felt duration of an activity simply does not track the clock, which is why effort alone rarely corrects it.

faq.q: Is time blindness an official ADHD symptom?
faq.a: It is not a standalone diagnostic criterion. Difficulties with time perception and estimation are widely described in connection with ADHD, and they also occur with sleep deprivation, depression and anxiety, so the experience by itself does not establish a diagnosis.

faq.q: Which rung should I start with?
faq.a: Start at Mark and Show. They cost almost nothing and they generate the record that the Measure and Correct rungs need. Starting at Correct without measurements means adjusting estimates by feel, which is the thing the ladder is designed to replace.

faq.q: Does this page diagnose or treat a health condition?
faq.a: No. It provides educational and organizational support only. Diagnosis and treatment belong to qualified professionals.

pages.h1: AI Business Coach: What It Can and Cannot Do
pages.definition: The AI Business Coach Capability Test is a five-part check for deciding what an AI business coach can be trusted with: whether it holds your context, challenges your framing, produces a decision rather than a summary, records what you committed to, and defers on questions it should not own.
pages.summary: An AI business coach is a structured prompting and record-keeping system, not a licensed advisor and not a person with a stake in your outcome. Its value depends almost entirely on whether it retains context and produces decisions you act on, which is what separates a coaching system from a chat window.
steps: Check whether it holds your context between sessions.
Check whether it challenges your framing instead of completing it.
Check whether it ends in a decision rather than a summary.
Check whether it records the commitment and returns to it unprompted.
Check whether it defers on the questions it should not own.
step_notes: A coach that starts from zero each session cannot notice patterns, and noticing patterns is most of what coaching is. Test it by referring to a constraint you mentioned previously without restating it. If the system needs the whole history pasted back every time, you are the one doing the retention.

Language models are built to continue what you give them, which makes them agreeable by default. A usable coaching setup has to be instructed to argue: to name the assumption your question depends on and to state the strongest case against the plan you arrived with.

"Here are five options to consider" is a summary. "Choose the second, because your stated constraint is cash and it is the only one that does not add fixed cost before March" is a decision. Ask for the recommendation and the reason it beats the alternative you were leaning toward.

Accountability is a record plus a return visit. If nothing is written down and nothing comes back to it, the arrangement produces good conversations and no follow-through, which is the most common way these systems quietly fail.

Legal exposure, tax positions, employment decisions, medical questions and anything with regulatory consequence belong with a qualified professional. A system that answers everything confidently is displaying a failure mode, not a capability.

Using it as a search box rather than as a standing arrangement.

failure_remedies: Fluent, confident prose is the one thing these systems reliably produce, and it is uncorrelated with whether the reasoning holds. Judge the output by whether the recommendation survives your strongest objection, not by how well it reads.

One-off questions produce one-off answers. The value comes from a repeating loop with the same retained context, a written commitment and a scheduled return, which is a workflow decision rather than a model capability.

Deference is a design requirement, not a limitation to work around. Decide in advance which categories go to a professional, and treat a confident answer inside those categories as a signal to stop relying on the system.

worked_example.title: A founder choosing between two hires
worked_example.text: A founder brings a hiring choice to a system that already holds their runway, current commitments and last quarter’s decisions. Rather than listing pros and cons, it names the assumption the question rests on — that both roles must be filled this quarter — recommends the operations hire because the stated constraint is the founder’s own calendar rather than revenue, and writes the decision with a review date. Three weeks later the founder is asked what happened to it.

limits: This is not licensed business, legal, tax or financial advice, and an AI system is not accountable for the outcome of a decision you take.
A coaching system cannot supply market knowledge it was never given, and it will produce confident answers well outside what your context supports.
pages.product_angle: Use the capability test to judge any AI coaching arrangement, including this one, before relying on it for consequential decisions.

faq.q: What is an AI business coach?
faq.a: It is a structured prompting and record-keeping arrangement built on a language model: it holds your context, asks questions against it, and keeps a record of what you decided. It is not a licensed advisor and has no stake in your outcome.

faq.q: Can an AI business coach replace a human coach?
faq.a: It replaces some of the function and none of the accountability. It is available on demand and cheap to run, and it has no independent read on you, no professional duty, and no consequence if the advice is wrong. The capability test is a way to decide which parts you are actually delegating.

faq.q: What should I never ask it to decide?
faq.a: Anything with legal, tax, employment, regulatory or medical consequence. A system that answers those confidently is exhibiting a failure mode rather than a capability, and appropriate deference is one of the five things worth testing before you rely on it.

faq.q: Does this framework guarantee an outcome?
faq.a: No. It creates a clearer process and evidence loop, but results depend on context, execution, resources, and decisions outside the framework.

pages.h1: AI Accountability Partner
pages.definition: The AI Accountability Loop is a six-part cycle that turns a language model into an accountability partner: checkable commitments, a fixed check-in, enough context to be challenged, a written record that includes misses, a pre-agreed response to a miss, and an escalation rule to a person.
pages.summary: An AI accountability partner works when it closes a loop: something committed, something checked, something recorded. Most attempts fail not because the model is weak but because nothing is written down and nothing returns to it, which leaves a supportive conversation and no accountability at all.
steps: Write each commitment in a form that can be checked rather than judged.
Fix a recurring check-in at the same time and in the same place.
Give the system the context it needs to challenge you, not just to agree.
Record every outcome in one place, including the misses.
Decide what happens after a miss before you miss.
Escalate to a person when the pattern stops being a planning problem.
step_notes: "Work on the deck" cannot be checked; "finish slides four to nine" can. A checkable commitment names an observable end state, so the check-in becomes a matter of fact rather than a negotiation about whether you tried hard enough. This single change does more than any prompt wording.

Accountability is created by the return visit, not by the promise. Put the check-in in the calendar at a fixed time and keep it in one conversation thread, so the system has continuity and you are not deciding each day whether to face it.

A model given only your plan will improve your plan. Give it the constraint you are avoiding — the deadline you doubt, the commitment you have already moved twice — and instruct it explicitly to name what you are dodging rather than to encourage you.

The record is the part that makes patterns visible, and misses are the entries that carry the information. A log containing only successes cannot show you that every third Wednesday collapses, which is precisely the finding that changes a plan.

Decide the recovery rule in advance: resume at the smallest valid unit, no catch-up debt, and one line explaining what blocked it. Deciding this while you are already behind guarantees the harshest available answer, which is what usually ends the arrangement.

A system that cannot start for three weeks running is not producing a planning problem. Persistent inability to act, or distress around it, is a reason to involve a person - a colleague, a coach, or a clinician - rather than to refine the prompt again.

failure_remedies: A commitment that cannot fail cannot hold you to anything, and it converts the check-in into a mood assessment. Rewrite it until a stranger reading it could tell you whether it was done.

Encouragement is the default behaviour, not a choice the system made about you. If you want the assumption named and the strongest counter-case stated, that has to be a standing instruction, repeated in the check-in itself.

Planning is the enjoyable half and produces nothing on its own. The loop only closes when a scheduled check-in reads back what was committed, which is why the calendar entry matters more than the prompt.

worked_example.title: A solo operator running a weekly loop
worked_example.text: An operator commits on Monday to sending three specific proposals by Thursday and logs it in one thread. The system is told the operator has moved this commitment twice already, and opens Thursday by asking which of the three were sent. Two were. The record notes the third was blocked by a missing price, the recovery rule resumes at the smallest unit rather than demanding all three, and the following Monday the system asks about the missing price before anything else is planned.

limits: This is an organizational support, not therapy, medical care, or licensed advice, and it is not a substitute for human relationships or professional help.
A language model has no stake in your outcome and no duty of care. It will not notice that you have quietly stopped returning unless the check-in is scheduled outside the conversation.
pages.product_angle: Use the loop as the operating cycle around any AI accountability setup, including this one.

faq.q: Does an AI accountability partner actually work?
faq.a: It works to the extent that it closes a loop: a checkable commitment, a scheduled return, and a written record. Where those three exist it functions as a reliable prompt to face what you said you would do. Where they are missing it produces a supportive conversation and no accountability.

faq.q: How is this different from just using ChatGPT to plan?
faq.a: Planning is a single pass; accountability requires the return visit. The difference is entirely in the check-in and the record, which live in your calendar and your log rather than in the model.

faq.q: What should I do when I miss a commitment?
faq.a: Apply the recovery rule you set in advance: resume at the smallest valid unit, add no catch-up work, and record one line about what blocked it. Deciding the response while you are already behind reliably produces the harshest answer, which is what ends most attempts.

faq.q: Does this framework guarantee an outcome?
faq.a: No. It creates a clearer process and evidence loop, but results depend on context, execution, resources, and decisions outside the framework.
